title: Tiny English Village Votes to 'Secede' From UK Over Asylum Centre Plan
excerpt: Piddington's 285-to-26 symbolic vote to become a 'principality' is the latest flashpoint in Britain's bitter fight over where to house asylum seekers.
body:
• Residents of Piddington, an Oxfordshire village of about 358 people, voted 285 to 26 on Tuesday in a symbolic referendum to seek independence from the United Kingdom.
  • The vote protests government plans to house up to 1,250 single adult male asylum seekers at the nearby former Bicester Garrison military site for at least a decade.
  • The result carries no legal weight, but villagers say it exposes the unfairness of placing a centre nearly four times the village's size beside a community with no shops, school or pub.
  • The Labour government insists the base will go ahead as it moves asylum seekers out of hotels; Prime Minister Andy Burnham says affluent areas must "play their part."

A village of 358 people in the Oxfordshire countryside has voted to leave the United Kingdom. On Tuesday, residents of Piddington cast ballots in a parish-council-organised referendum on whether to "seek to secede from the United Kingdom and pursue self-determination" — and on Wednesday the result was announced: 285 in favour, 26 against, with one spoiled ballot from 312 counted, a turnout of nearly 92 percent. The target: a government plan to house up to 1,250 single adult male asylum seekers at the Bicester Garrison, a disused military depot less than a mile away, for at least ten years. The vote has no legal standing, but the council has declared the "principality of Piddington" — a nod to the 1949 Ealing comedy Passport to Pimlico, in which Londoners declare independence.

Context & Background

Piddington, 15 miles from Oxford and recorded in the Domesday Book, has a 12th-century church and a village hall with a monthly pop-up pub — but no shop, café, school or post office. Residents say a centre holding nearly four times the village's population would overwhelm it. "For us, it's about proportionality — how does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?" parish council chair Tim McNally told Sky News, accusing the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through." Villager Ian Darby, 63, told AFP the village was willing to take a share of migrants but considered 1,200 excessive: "It's all about how do we get our voice heard in a different way." Seventy-six-year-old Herbert Owen said he voted to leave because the government did not "care"; 17-year-old Dita Jackson said, "I won't really feel safe enough to walk around anymore." Announcing the result, Susannah Parden declared: "We are Piddington, the village that roars."

Impact & Analysis

The vote lands in Britain's most combustible debate. Some 101,900 people applied for asylum in 2025, the third-highest ever, per government figures cited by CNN. Andy Burnham's Labour government, in power since July 2024, is moving asylum seekers out of costly hotels — a policy inherited from the Conservatives — into former military bases, vowing to end hotel use by 2029. The shift has met fierce resistance: on September 5–6, masked demonstrators blocked traffic at Dover and hundreds of balaclava-wearing protesters clashed with police in Portsmouth after a migrant boat landed, CNN reported. The government is holding its line. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told the BBC a former military base "is a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels: "We do have to house people somewhere while we get a grip on the asylum chaos... and that base will go ahead." Burnham told GB News he would "look into" Piddington's concerns but said affluent areas must "play their part" rather than leaving dispersal to the poorest communities.

"For us, it's about proportionality — how does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?"

— Tim McNally, chair, Piddington parish council

"We do have to house people somewhere while we get a grip on the asylum chaos... and that base will go ahead."

— Lisa Nandy, UK Culture Secretary

Oxfordshire council leader Tim Bearder praised campaigners but warned the centre "will be a lightning rod to the far right." And there are practical doubts: The Times reports a Home Office assessment found no viable gas network, limited water and "largely non-operational" drainage at the site — raising the prospect of delays.

Diaspora Angle

For the UK's large Indian diaspora, the episode is a barometer of how heated Britain's immigration debate has become. When protests turn confrontational and council leaders warn of far-right flashpoints, the political temperature rises for everyone with a migration story.

What's Next

Legally, nothing changes, and ministers say the plan will proceed — though the infrastructure problems now on the record give opponents ammunition to slow it. Cherwell district council says migrants could still arrive at the garrison later this year or in early 2027. The bigger question is whether the "principality" becomes a template: with thousands of asylum seekers slated for former military sites, other villages will be watching closely.
